This bill, which appears to be insignificant, with just two pages and one clause which amends the Railway Act and something called "at and east", is a complete mystery to most members of this House. Yet, for those of us from Atlantic Canada, the "at and east" provision of that Railway Act that is being abolished by Bill C-26 is as fundamental to us in Atlantic Canada for the export and the movement of grain as the Crow's Nest Pass was in western Canada.
I am very embarrassed that a government would bring this on without consultations with all the affected parties, as has been promised. We heard it was going to be brought forward last Thursday. Having checked with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council today, there has been no response to them from the ministry to discuss something that Atlantic Canadians, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission and most of the Atlantic members were prepared to accept.
We understood there needed to be change in the "at and east" subsidy, a subsidy that was valued at $35 million in direct payments to the railways to pay the difference between a frozen rate in the 1960 climate of freight rates and the compensatory rate which obviously is a higher rate. That difference is a subsidy of about $35 million. It is quite correct, this is a budget item which, of course, is another element which gives me some concern in view of other things that have happened with budgets around here.
The sad thing is that the Atlantic community most affected by this and Atlantic members on all sides, especially the government side, have been waiting to see what was going to come from something called "offsets". "Offsets" is about as mysterious as the words "at and east". The offsets are offsets that could be done by cabinet order involving one, two or three ministers to, in effect, offset the loss of the subsidy by doing some other things, for instance, removing the tariff on the importation of American com. That itself would help somewhat to redress the loss of the subsidy.
There was to be some type of agreement with unit trains from the lakehead eastward. There were to be many things, and yet none of that has happened even though we have known about a change.
April 30, 1990

In fact, to give full credit where credit is due, it was the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission itself that came up with a proposal in 1985 suggesting changes in the subsidy. It realized that this government was trying to reduce a deficit. It was trying to be sensible and reasonable and came up with a formula to reduce the subsidy from $35 million to approximately $10 million with consequential offsets to come into place.
That was 1985. It has not happened. There has not been any movement. There has not been any response. There have been some letters. Perhaps the problem is that it involves three or four ministers of the Crown and/or the Atlantic Province Transportation Commission and the Maritime Farmers Council, but there has not been any response to the most reasonable, responsible reaction to this element of at and east which we all knew needed change.
The Budget Papers say that this is one of the subsidy programs that has outlived its usefulness because now Atlantic ports are competitive with American ports. The phrase "at and east" was introduced to have Atlantic ports competitive at and east of Buffalo with American ports, i.e., the ports of Saint John and Halifax would be competitive. That was one of the reasons for the at and east subsidy and that has been recognized by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council.
There is another reason, which I know is going to surprise some members of this House, why there was an at and east proposal and this was never even touched on in the Budget Papers. I will go back to the initial debate on this bill in the Transport Committee in 1966. A fellow called Mr. Pickersgill, the then Minister of Transport, came before that committee and said certain things.
We honour my friend from Regina-Lumsden today. It is his birthday and he is going to get into the hallowed halls of retirees and pensioners. He has been a most diligent, constructive, and sometimes cantankerous member of the transport committee for 21 years, but he has always brought an insight on transport matters which I wish was shared by all members of this House. I compliment him for that.
This took place just before the member came along the pike, but I happened to be there. Mr. Pickersgill appeared before the transport committee on Thursday, October 6, 1966.
Government Orders
To digress for a minute, I wish that some members of this House on all sides would start to pay attention a little more to many aspects of our history. Quite frankly, if we looked at some of our history perhaps we would not have some of the problems that we have today.
Mr. Pickersgill, the then Minister of Transport, came before the transport committee on Thursday, October 6, to explain this mammoth change in transportation. In fact, it was the new transportation policy, it set up the national transportation agency. It was the new blueprint which was not changed until the Deputy Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport when we took over, brought in the new transportation act. About the at and east rates Mr. Pickersgill said, among other things:
The one other thing that affects the Atlantic provinces, in this Bill especially, is something that has never been done before, and that is the underwriting of the so-called "At and East Rates", which are the rates on grain between the lakeports and ports from Montreal east, including and being of particular importance to Halifax and Saint John. According to the Board of Transport Commissioners, these rates are already unremunerative. In the year 1966 the railways already have been paid some compensation for maintaining these rates. We have decided to keep those rates at their present level and to pay compensation for doing so. This is because we feel there is an equal obligation in this field to the obligation with regard to the Crowsnest. The purpose of this is to ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports. This might be a debatable question but, at any rate, it is the policy embodied in this bill and I think, on balance, when we consider the terms of the Atlantic Development Board study on the ports of Halifax and Saint John, as to the effects of the increased St. Lawrence transportation, it is one very desirable offset in that field.
That explanation extends the reason why there ever was an at and east. It was not just to be competitive with American ports. It was so that Halifax and Saint John could be competitive with the St. Lawrence ports. The St. Lawrence ports are still there. They still get the benefit of coast guard, ice navigation and many elements from the Department of Transport, and I do not quibble with that. But what I do take exception to is that in his budget speech the Minister of Finance mentioned only one reason why the subsidy was there. He is right that it is not necessary any more, because of containers and everything else, for that subsidy between Atlantic ports and the eastern ports at and east of Buffalo on the American side. But it is still very necessary for Saint John and Halifax in terms of the St. Lawrence ports that are still very much there and still very much get help from the federal government through many programs.

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
I, as one Canadian from Atlantic Canada, cannot accept Bill C-26 in its present form, especially with no assurance that there are going to be offsets, because we still have something from your neck of the woods, Mr. Speaker, and from the neck of the woods of my hon. friend from Regina-Lumsden. We still have something call the Western Grain Transportation Act which distorts the movement of grain to the tune of about $850 million. I am aware of some of that history. I know there are some moves to try to reform and revise that, to perhaps give some of that money to the producers rather than paying it to the railways. There are many different things being discussed.
Well let us discuss them and try to define where we make the change. But is it fair to make the change on the little $35 million in Bill C-26 that hits Atlantic Canada right in the gonads and not do anything to the Western Grain Transportation Act which affects the western farmers to the tune of $850 million? That is not fair or equitable and that is why Bill C-26 should not be before this House at second reading until there is something done.
As I said earlier, we had the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission before the Transport Committee on February 22. They are so reasonable. In fact, I talked to the chairman afterwards and said that he most likely shot himself in both feet let alone knee-capping himself because he did not come out a little more critically of the fact that since 1985 there has been no response fundamentally to the proposals they put forward then for offsets. They were so reasonable that they said they had looked at some of those offsets and they think that perhaps they are not in the complete balance that should be applied, and they came up with another proposal. They came up with a proposal that removes the subsidy on an ongoing yearly basis and only ties it to the three winter months when, in effect, the St. Lawrence is closed and the Atlantic ports could still get the benefit of the flow of grain to the east as long as they got the subsidy to help pay the difference between the frozen rate and the compensatory rate that the railways would charge.
I just wanted to put on the record that this is much more than just a subsidy to be competitive with American ports. It is part of our national dimension. It is part of the fabric which keeps this country together. Mr. Pearson said many years ago in this Chamber that there is a price to pay to have a Canada. He was referring to the
questions about the cost of bilingualism. There are so many costs to keep this country together from coast to coast.
One of the little elements that helped us in Atlantic Canada was at and east. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, on its own without pressure from the federal government, came through with suggestions to reduce that subsidy to about $10 million if there was movement on the offsets.
I want to put on the record what we are talking about when we talk about offsets. I understand that the problem is that there are four or five ministers involved and perhaps not one minister has tried to address this. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, that those of us in Atlantic Canada cannot stay quiet anymore on this unless we have some assurance that those offsets are going to come into play.
I quoted Mr. Pickersgill who brought in the national transportation bill and then became the first chairman of the national transportation agency. That was a very good bill for him. But he did something good for Atlantic Canada on the at and east. For us to let that go and quietly wait for some action on the offsets is not correct for any of us from Atlantic Canada. It puts members on all sides, and especially the government side, in a very embarrassing position.
I am not talking about the moon. I am not talking about the expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars in terms of offsets. Do you know what I am talking about? I am talking about unit trains to move the export grain to Halifax and Saint John, the use of water transport for the shipment of Plan "C" feed grains to Atlantic Canada, the elimination of the countervail and duty on U.S. com, provision of facilities to receive grain by water at Saint John, promotion of the continued use of Halifax for the shipment of export flour and provision of permits allowing the importation of feed grains from foreign countries. Just about all of those things involve not only two or three ministers of the government but-and this is fundamental-involve the co-operation and the action of the Canadian Wheat Board.
Often, for understandable reasons, to protect the credibility of our wheat, to make sure we had a hard durum that did not have imperfections and was not going to be diluted with soft grains, the Canadian Wheat Board, for so many years, has maintained that very proper control of the wheat trade. But there comes a time, when you are trying to help one area of the country, when quite frankly we do not need the Durum
April 30,1990

wheats and the hard cereal grains in the west, we need the soft grains and feed grains in the east.
In the meantime, we need some help at the export level to keep the elevators at Saint John and Halifax, because if you do not have elevators in Saint John and Halifax you are not going to have the wherewithal to keep these feed grains that you can develop in Atlantic Canada. That is the bottom line that is so disastrous, to have this bill come into effect with no action on the offsets.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission is as sad as I am that they have had no communication whatsoever, I am told, since they wrote after their appearance before our committee on Februaiy 20, 1990. I find that regrettable at best. Perhaps I had better watch what I think at the worst, because I just cannot understand that.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission came before the committee and said that they understand some of the difficulties the government is having and are prepared to suggest a new change for offsets. I want to get this on the record so that someone somewhere in the bureaucracy can finally read it because perhaps it has not got around. After all, it was only February, 1990, and perhaps it has not had time to circulate around and be addressed.
The proposal that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission laid before the transport committee for the first time caught us all by surprise. It is as follows:
In lieu of "At and East" and proposed only to apply on an annual
basis during period of seaway winter closing:
(i)	rail rates on export grain and flour to Halifax/Saint John be set at a fixed rate differential over St. Lawrence ports at a level necessary to make the Maritime ports competitive with St. Lawrence ports and to encourage the use of the Maritime ports and the railways serving these ports;
(ii)	railways to be reimbursed by subsidy for the difference between the "fixed" rate level and compensatory rates;
(iii)	facilities to receive grain by water at the Saint John elevator be provided; and
(iv)	to prevent undue burden on the federal treasury-
These are not politicians talking, this is the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission trying to get something in place to help us. Out west they have the tariff off of com. I see colleagues of mine from the west. The parliamentary secretary is from the west. Why should they have the removal of the corn tariff in British
Government Orders
Columbia when we still have it hanging around our throats in Nova Scotia and Atlantic Canada? That is part of the other discrimination.
To continue my mild remarks on their reasonable proposal, they say:
(iv) to prevent undue burden on the federal treasury, the special provision for "fixed" rates could be limited to maximum tonnages both for export grain and flour but not less than the volume required to maintain the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John and the flour mill at Halifax as viable operations.
They end up their note by saying:
The APTC would be prepared to work with federal officials to
assist with the development and implementation of these proposals.
That is dated February 19, 1990. That is a variation of what they presented in 1985, and we had not heard. Can I stay here and stay silent as a member from Atlantic Canada when we have not even heard?
This is second reading and this is going to go to a committee. I wish one of the four ministers responsible for resolving these offsets was in the House. There was one but he has left. I wish there was a minister involved in the hoped for discussion on this issue who, before this debate concludes, could come into the House and give some assurance that there is going to be action on the offsets, perhaps not to the total satisfaction of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, but at least some action.
That memo to the transport committee was dated Februaiy 19 and they came on Februaiy 20 and presented their evidence and in effect supplemented what they said.
I certainly cannot support this bill at this time. I am only hoping that some sense is going to come to the ministers involved to address this serious issue. You are from western Canada, Mr. Speaker, and have been a valued member of this House for many years, as is my friend from Regina-Lumsden.
I just cannot believe that a government would bring in a bill affecting the Crowsnest Pass without a lot more deliberation, especially when there was an agency that was willing to work out a resolution of the difficulties with the loss of the subsidy. Their proposal, on their own figures, and I have not heard a rebuttal yet from the federal officials, is to reduce this subsidy on their own from $35 million to about $10 million. That $10 million means the future of the elevators in Saint John and

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
Halifax, the feed situation in Atlantic Canada and what that does to our farmers in Atlantic Canada.
Quite frankly, there are some people in Atlantic Canada who suggest that in Atlantic Canada we should not even try to raise feed grains. I am not going to go that far.
I just want to conclude by saying that never in my experience has an agency so affected by a budget matter been so reasonable, frankly I think almost to their own detriment, in not trying to organize Atlantic members in a much more aggressive way to speak on their behalf, to ensure that there is some type of offset. You have heard about the offsets that we are talking about. They are all by Order in Council with the co-operation of the Wheat Board, and yet nothing has happened.
There should not be any mystery as to why this member on this side cannot support this legislation at this time. I am only hoping that when we get this into committee, those officials charged with looking at these offsets since 1985 can indicate what they have been doing since then and/or what they have been doing since February 19, 1990.

Mr. Speaker, I rise very briefly just to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. I am sure the people of Nova Scotia and and of the Atlantic region will be delighted to hear his comments today, comments that have been echoed on this side of the House by other members from Atlantic Canada. Perhaps my hon. friend has realized that if we do not hang together we certainly will hang separately.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments of the hon. member for Halifax. She could have rubbed it in even a little further. She did not really rub it in the way she could have. Quite frankly, as far as I am concerned, as some of my colleagues on this side of the House know, we have to really start to practise some of the reforms in the McGrath report with regard to issues, not on the partisan things that we run elections on, but on subject matter. This was never an issue in an election. Obviously if it had been and my party had this position
and I got elected, I would not be standing up here opposing it.
But I think the only way this place is ever going to survive is if we can have some repartee and exchanges on all sides of the House on different issues where government confidence is not involved. I appreciate that this matter is a budget item. There are different degrees of budget items but, notwithstanding that it is a budget item, I still think that on so many issues members have to start saying what they believe and let the chips fall where they may.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment the hon. member, my colleague and the chairman of the transport committee. I appreciated his remarks about my birthday and service in the committee. When I get cantankerous it is usually because of the chairman.
This bill amends an ordinary statute, the Railway Act. It may have been announced in the budget but it is not a budget bill. How does he make that a budget bill? I submit that this bill is not a matter of confidence. There are occasions when members from all sides, including government members, as a last resort, can decide to let the government and the government House Leader know that they must withdraw a bill or change it or they will vote against it or stay out or something.
Does he not agree that this is one of those rare opportunities when members can do as Liberal members failed to do on the Crowsnest Pass rates when they went along with getting rid of them?
For a matter of sheer survival, if nothing else, I would think government members from Atlantic Canada should be ready to say, "Look, withdraw this bill or substantially change it or we are not going to be here to vote or we are going to vote against it". It is not an issue of confidence. How does the member say that this bill is a matter of confidence?

I will be very quick because I know other members want to speak. My friend shows his experience here in the House. All I said was it came down in the budget. I might have said a budgetary proposal, but there is no ways and means motion. I said I could not support it as it is. Whether I vote against it or not is something I have to decide. I am certainly not going to be here to support it the way it is.
April 30, 1990

I will be horrified if there are very many Atlantic members, other than the members of the cabinet, who have read the bill and understand the implications of it, who would support this bill going through now. I would have no hesitation supporting this bill if we could come up with the offsets. Frankly, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission and others in the Atlantic farm community understood our position.
We have the bill before us now and there has been no action on the offsets. I quite agree with the hon. member. I am just not going to support it as is.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lewis that Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies) be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and on the amendment of Ms. Clancy (p. 8227).

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that we did not quickly adjourn this time and are giving a fair hearing, in some ways, to Bill C-26. It is not quite as fair as it should be in that the rules for implementation of this bill were carried forth last summer. It is not fair because the government directed the rail subsidies to be altered last July. It is not fair to everyone involved. Nevertheless, it is a bill that has been brought forward by the government.

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
What in fact is the at and east legislation or Bill C-26? In 1960 the Liberal government realized that various subsidies had to be put in place in order to help the areas at or east of Buffalo to compete with American ports and harbours which were sending grain to Europe and other areas. Also, it was to help them compete with Montreal and the harbours in that area. All grain subsidies were looked at and there were some rules set aside.
Some rail rates were put in place so that communities at and east of Buffalo would be able to reasonably compete with other areas of the country. The ports that were eligible for at and east until last summer were Halifax, Montreal, St. John's and areas east of Montreal. The grains that were subsidized at that point were wheat, wheat flour, oats, buckwheat, barley, rye, com and soya beans.
We all recall the budget of March or April 1989 when the Canadian government seemed to change its total perspective on what was happening in agriculture. The legislation that came down at that point must have been written by the Minister of Agriculture in the United States. If we stop and think about what in fact it stated, in 1989 it removed $90 million from crop insurance programs across this country. This year it will be $110 million. It changed our branch line rehabilitation or our rehabilitation of rail lines that carry agricultural products by $46 million in 1989 and $2 million in 1990. It changed our advance payments to crops in 1989 by $27 million and in 1990-91 it was the same, $27 million.
Dairy export subsidies were cut by $5 million in 1989 and $7 million in 1990. The farm credit cuts were $6 million in 1989 and $8.5 million in 1990. The fuel tax rebate was cut by $42 million in 1989 and $125 million this year. All of those cuts that were engineered after the free trade agreement were not designed for the betterment of Canadian agriculture but were designed for other reasons. All of those cuts were not done by the U.S., but by the Canadian government to Canadian farmers.
The at and east bill was put in place, a bill which cut $20 million in rail subsidies in 1989 and $40 million in total by 1990. The government says that it listens to Canadians. It may listen to Canadians but certainly its actions are anti what it hears. Its actions are very much against the Canadian agricultural community. These are actions very much against the solid environment that we
had in agriculture and are bringing it down more and more.
Before the election the present government suggested Canada was in a very healthy condition. They were going to put billions of dollars into helping agriculture and billions of dollars for all kinds of programs. Suddenly, after the election, we saw a very bleak picture.
We heard all we could about the debt and the deficit. We heard all about all of the difficulties that have come about in Canada. Not once was that mentioned during the election campaign. Not once was the dire effect of this budget, which cut in almost every area of agriculture, ever mentioned. Was it part of the agenda for free trade? Many people in this country strongly believe that to be the fact. Was it something that was given up at a point? Many people believe that.
In 1985 the Atlantic Provincial Transportation Commission made some very strong statements about what should happen to the program at and east. It suggested the government take no action on the at and east because it would create some serious problems in Canada. Its warning suggested that the serious economic impacts would hurt agriculture, the longshoremen and the elevator system in the east, as well as across Canada.
It suggested that the loss to the maritimes alone, if the at and east program were removed would be $27 million. It suggested that hundreds and hundreds of jobs would be lost in the Atlantic provinces, let alone the hundreds of jobs that will be lost throughout Canada as a result of this program being cut.
Capital purchases for milling ports would be lost by those who are involved in the milling of grains, not only in Ontario but throughout the eastern area. Livestock feed for cattle will certainly escalate in price when the grains that are shipped there are no longer subsidized, but are shipped in at a much higher cost. Certainly, the elevator workers in Saint John have lost their jobs because of the closing of the major elevator there.
The at and east program affects not only the east, but Ontario as well. The Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board has made some pretty strong statements about the problems with the at and east program. The at and east program did allow orderly marketing for those who were involved in the wheat program, and if you were in an area where you harvested all of your grain within approximately a four week period, that grain was shipped to market.
April 30, 1990

If you do not have a program in place that will help the shipment of grain at different times of the year, after the freeze of the lake or after other low prices of grain are there, we all know that when we take grain off during those four weeks, there is a tremendous amount on the market. The price drops quite dramatically. However, three, four, five, or six months later, the price of grain escalates quite dramatically.
To make it fair for those producers to sell their grain, not all at one time as though everyone is dumping it at the same time, a grain transportation program was put in place and elevator programs were put in place so that the grain could be taken to elevators on Georgian Bay or to other areas of Canada, stored there until such time that the price of grain improved and the grain could be sold.
With this particular bill coming into place, of three elevators on Georgian Bay, one has already been sold and two are up for sale at this point in time. This indicates that that orderly marketing, that chance that they have to sell grain throughout the winter and through the next spring, is lost. We also know that there is insufficient storage for grains in Canada and, without a grain transportation bill, those depots, those storage areas will diminish and as a result the Canadian farmer, the grain producer in particular, is going to be in a more difficult situation.
Non-availability of rail structures means a great deal to the demise of the price of wheat throughout the Canadian production. Ontario wheat producers produce
700,000	tonnes of wheat, 450,000 tonnes of which is exported at the best market price possible. As a result, there will be bottlenecks and stoppages where producers will not be able to gain the best market for their grain.
The government, in undermining the at and east bill, also moves along to undermine orderly marketing. Removal of at and east places in jeopardy the ability to move and export grains to customers in many different regions as well. The Ontario Wheat Producers' Marketing Board indicated that the program will totally undermine the orderly marketing procedure. What the at and east program would in fact do or has done is diminish the
Government Orders
chances of bottlenecking of products and sales all at one time.
Let us look back at the issue of free trade. As the government continues down its unilateral process to reduce the agriculture programs and subsidies that have been in place for several years, the U.S. has not taken one step in dealing with its programs and its subsidies. The Atlantic Provincial Transportation Commission has recommended the removal of countervail duties on American com. Reactions such as this not only hurt the existing situation, but damage the economy in other parts of Canada.
If we allow American grain into Canada, the Atlantic producers, Ontario producers or western producers will suffer a great deal of hardship. This program seems to divide our country quite dramatically. It pits one area against another. Those kinds of issues should have been taken into account before this transportation bill was brought into effect.
Even though the at and east subsidy was announced in 1989 and the bill was not presented until June 1989, subsidies ceased on July 26, 1989. We are now debating the bill in April, going on May 1990, when subsidies were cut last July. We certainly have to look at the government and its respect for the parliamentary process.
Railroads have been instructed to take their lost subsidies into account as of July 1989. The government bypassed the House of Commons and bypassed the parliamentary process in doing such. Why are we here debating nine months after the actions of the bill have been taken? It seems quite ridiculous and quite unacceptable that we are in this position at this time. This government continues to do that type of thing. It not only loses credibility with the Canadian public but it loses credibility with everyone involved in any programs. At any time the government can retroactively cancel a program and take back the money or subsidies that have been put in place by bills or other measures.
People functioning under many of our programs have to be very confused and upset. They have to wonder whether the grant they are receiving is going to be

April 30,1990
Government Orders
carried through properly or if the government going to ask for pay-backs at a later time.
When the government placed the GST ads in newspapers, we suggested that it was overlooking the view of Parliament. With this it seems much worse. The actions were put in place nine months before the bill was debated in the House of Commons and that is a shame. The government has suggested there will be a saving of $40 million. That is misleading. It is a false saving. If the maritime economy suffers, as it has, then we must pay unemployment insurance to help those who have been foisted out of their jobs. We have to look at the extra costs to the producers of chickens, pork and beef who have to pay extra funding for the grains that they feed to their animals. Then, somebody else is paying the bill. Much the same way that the finance minister foisted expenses on to the provinces, he is again here foisting expenses onto other areas of government and foisting expenses on to other production areas in the maritimes. It is costing somebody that extra money. Certainly it is costing in the wrong way, a non-productive way.
pushing the farm community aside when our counterparts are doing just the opposite? The U.S. is more highly subsidizing. Certainly, I know of no program where it has taken away the profits, the subsidies, the help that it has given its farmers. Was it an agreement that was made before? Is it just the realism of the free trade agreement that is coming down on paper, things that we were not aware of that were discussed and put in motion in 1988 which are now being placed?
I am not clear, but as I look at our budgets, as I look at what is happening to agriculture and as I look at the pressures that are coming through Canada, I feel very strongly that Canada, particularly in agriculture and transportation, is strongly under attack.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act with respect to the grain and flour subsidies.

We need to have programs in this country which really bring about better production, not cut jobs, not cut security, not cut agriculture. The maritime economy has been very hard hit lately. We all know that. Adding extra costs to the livestock and poultry feed costs is no option. The loss of milling quality wheat in the maritimes will result from this bill. When we are already suffering the loss of VIA Rail, losses in the fishing industry and high unemployment, that is very unacceptable to me and I am certain it is unacceptable to you, Mr. Speaker, that the government now foists another problem on the maritimes.
Ontario will also be affected. The Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board has made its comments on how it will be affected. All of Canadian agriculture will suffer, particularly at this time. We face low prices and we face a great deal of pressure and demand from the U.S. free trade agreement. We are suffering as a result of world subsidies on grains, and certainly as a result of the battle between the United States and the European markets.
Why is Canada at this time taking away the support we had for this very valuable agricultural industry and
This bill before us is but one in a series of measures announced in the 1989 budget by this government, which has the effect of harming Canadian farmers, dismantling piece by piece the underpinnings of orderly agriculture marketing, and abandoning Atlantic Canada once again.
Like many other pieces of legislation introduced by this government, the elimination of the at and east subsidy is ill-conceived. Like many other pieces of legislation introduced by the government, this bill has as much to do with this government's mistaken approach to free trade as it does with deficit reduction. The way in which this government has proceeded with this measure is an insult to our respect for democracy and the rule of law. In the strictest sense, the at and east program allows for the shipment of grain and flour to ports east of and including Montreal, by rail, at a fixed rate. The program's cost is $40 million annually.
In a report by the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board we read about the at and east: "In due consideration of the economics associated with the at and east program, as applied to the total marketing process, the Ontario Wheat Board considers the program to be invaluable to its operation and to the interests of all facets of the industry". It went on to say that for the amount of dollars extended in the subsidy program, it
: V;

April 30, 1990

may be the best and least expensive insurance plan available to the eastern marketing system.
The government has decided that the at and east program should be eliminated. We on this side ask why the government is doing this? It is possible the government just did not have all the facts when it announced its intention to eliminate the program in the 1989 budget.
The members opposite did not truly understand the purpose of the program, the conditions which make its continued relevancy, and the benefits the program brings to many regions of the country and sectors of our economy. I trust they are listening to the arguments being made not only by myself and my colleagues but mostly by the Ontario wheat farmers, a number of whom from my own riding who are calling on this government to withdraw this bill.
There is little question that the government made a serious error of omission in identifying the original intention of the at and east program. In announcing its planned elimination, the government stated: "The intent of the program was to ensure that Canadian grain and flour shipments would continue to be exported through Canadian east coast ports, rather than competing U.S. ports". That is all the government said.
In fact, the intention of the government of the day in bringing in this program was twofold, not just for that reason. In addition to ensuring that eastern Canadian ports could compete with U.S. ports, the program intended to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to complete the ports of the St. Lawrence.
In 1966, the then transport minister said: "We feel there is an equal obligation in this field with regard to the Crowsnest. The purpose of this is to ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports".
This omission is very important because it nullifies the government's contention that the program is no longer needed because the conditions which justify it no longer exist. One of the two reasons given by the government for its elimination is just plain wrong.
The second government justification for the program's elimination is equally misguided, but much more erro-
Govemment Orders
neous than the first. The budget papers read: "The subsidy has the effect of diverting traffic away from the Seaway in favour of subsidized rail movements and is inconsistent with the government's market-oriented policy". The government uses the term "market-oriented" as a banner, more like a shield to hide behind. These are the government's catch phrases, as though their mere invocation should be enough to stifle dissent, lest a government critic be labelled a socialist.
The fact of the matter is that this government has brought the term "market-oriented" and the term "free trade" along with it into the realms of obscurity. These terms now mean anything the government wants them to mean. Most often, that spells hardship for Canadian farmers.
The Canadian government has embarked on the path of unilateral disarmament. In the wake of the free trade agreement and in the midst of agricultural negotiations at GATT, as well as in the expectation of the subsidy negotiations with the United States, the members opposite and the government are stripping the country of programs that have served us so well. Prior to any negotiations with the free trade agreement, it was giving away the boat.
The at and east program obviously is one of these programs that should be protected, but that the government is giving up prior to negotiations on subsidies for the free trade deal. The program has resulted in benefits to Atlantic ports in the elevators of Saint John and Halifax. The at and east forms a vital part of the orderly and efficient marketing of its grain by providing control over its movement of exports.
It is a system that has benefited exporters of Canadian wheat by providing a year-round supply, while at the same time, benefiting producers by protecting them from forcing to sell their wheat at a fixed time, even if that time coincides with a temporary drop in the world price. The at and east has also enabled grain producers to more efficiently utilize the limited storage and elevator space in the Georgian Bay and Great Lakes regions. It has helped to alleviate the problems of bottle-neck and congestion within our transportation system. The at and east had facilitated the development of a storage and transportation system that served producers and consumers well at very little cost to the government in real terms.

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
As the Ontario Wheat Board has stated:
The fact that non-availability of rail facilities during harvest forces
the Ontario Wheat Board to use lakeside transfer elevators within the
boundaries of Ontario in itself justifies the at and east as the board's
only economical movement to winter markets.
While the U.S. and the EEC trade war continues to strongly depress world wheat prices, what does this government do but cut out a $40 million annual program which has created jobs, increased storage capacity and formed a cornerstone of orderly marketing.
This program has done much to help the Ontario wheat producer. The elimination of the program could increase the board's marketing cost by approximately $3 million per year. Normally, they would have moved up to
110,000	tonnes out of Georgian Bay port elevators to the east coast export position by rail at $5.50 a tonne. In the absence of the program the rate may go as high as $32 a tonne.
The Georgian Bay elevators provide almost 25 per cent available storage capacity to the Ontario industry. If the loss of program leads to those elevators becoming non-economic then the board will be forced to export earlier or develop other storage alternatives. Clearly, there will be a loss of jobs and a loss of the ability of Ontario farmers to to export their wheat in an orderly manner. If the government was committed to ending the program it would have been preferable to phase out the rate assistance over a period of two or three years while at the same time negotiating more competitive rates with the railways.
This government has failed, time and time again, to consult with those who would be most adversely affected by it. As a result, it has been detrimental to the ability of these people to export to their markets in a reasonable way.
The point cannot be lost on producers that the budget change falls in line with the elimination of the two-priced wheat system and a commitment in the free trade agreement to open up Canadian markets to U.S. grains. Have the Americans been stripping their farmers of agricultural exports? No, they have not.
I have been talking about the at and east in the present tense, as though it were still around and there was a chance to change the government's mind after informed debate.
The fact is that members opposite have already done away with the program. They could not be bothered with the democratic process. Clauses 1.1 and 4.1 contain deeming provisions. Even before the bill had been debated in the House the government put the word out that all contracts signed after July, 1989, nine months ago, would not be converted by the at and east. I quote from a letter by the director of rail freight programs. He says:
The deeming provisions are intended to assure that the effective date of this measure will be July 16,1989, even if final parliamentary approval comes later.
That is no way to run a government. That is no way to run a democracy. I believe that this sentence and the attitude it betrays is an insult to each of us in this House. The government seems at times bored and impatient with parliamentary democracy. It does not seem to be listening. It does not take the time to ask before it acts. Had it listened, it might have realized that there were ways to alter the at and east program to better serve Canadians, not needlessly harm them.
I could go on about its effect on agriculture in the maritimes but I understand my friend, the member for Dartmouth, will be talking about that shortly. In closing, we on this side do not appreciate the way the government has dealt with this issue.
The government should not try to reduce the debt and the deficit on the backs of the farming community and rural Canada. If that is its intention, it should first negotiate and talk with those who would be adversely affected by such a program and, in that way, try to alleviate some of the hardship that these programs would cause.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment my colleague, the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk, on his excellent speech and intervention on this piece of legislation. I want to draw particular attention to his very cogent suggestions about the way in which a reconsideration of the at and east subsidy program could have been approached by this government, rather than the hamhanded fashion in which it was carried out, with no consultation, and effectively cutting the rates without even bringing the matter before Parliament. That is something that I discussed in my own remarks today.
April 30, 1990

I would like to ask the member to elaborate on some of the points that he has made, particularly from his perspective as a member representing an agricultural riding in southern Ontario. What effects would the bill have on the producers in his area? What alternative arrangements have been proposed that were not considered by this government?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for that question.
Today, farmers in my area are facing hard times, and this is just one more attack by this government on the farming communities in our country. Wheat producers in my area can use the at and east in differing ways. The main advantage of the at and east for wheat producers in my area is to assure that they can market their product in an orderly fashion. This means that they can hold onto their product and get just that little higher price for it than they might be able to get otherwise.
That small profit allows them to survive as farmers. Farmers in my constituency and, indeed, farmers across Canada live on the edge. A $40 million program may not mean a lot to a government that is intent on reducing the debt and reducing the deficit, but it means a great deal to my farmers who only earn that little bit. It means the difference between having a viable farm operation and actually having to get out of farming all together.
I thank my hon. colleague for asking me that question because I think it is an important one. I do not think that members opposite realize how much a $40 million program could mean to the viability of farming in southwestern Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on Bill C-26.
At the outset let me join with you, Sir, in your compliments to my colleague, the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden who, as you duly noted, celebrated his 65th birthday yesterday. He is a veteran of this House and a veteran of the transport committee, with at least 21 years of continuous service.
I know all members will agree that while they may not have agreed with his positions, he certainly has done yeoman service on behalf of transportation. He is very happy to once again be battling a bill that is designed to take away services in transportation, as the Liberal
Government Orders
government did with its bill to end the Crow benefit. Now, the irony of ironies is that on his birthday, the Conservative government is now attacking the at and east freight assistance program.
I also want to compliment my colleague, the member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre, a new member in this House who has dual responsibilities as grain and oilseeds critic and transportation critic for grain. He has done an overwhelming job in preparing for this bill and for the debates that have taken place. I do want to thank him as well for his fine work.
The at and east freight assistance program pays a subsidy to the railways on export grain and flour moving by specified routes through eastern Canadian ports. The rates paid by the shipper have been frozen since 1960 with respect to export grain and 1966 with respect to flour. It is primarily grains and flour that is coming from the west, through the port of Thunder Bay, through the Great Lakes to the bay ports, to some of the lower St. Lawrence ports and eventually railed through to Atlantic Canada to the elevators there.
Some of it does go by rail from Thunder Bay under the flour subsidy component and is taken by train through to Atlantic Canada. The program freezes bulk rates from any rail point along Georgian Bay, Lake Huron, or any waterways directly or indirectly connecting with Lake Huron and not farther east than Prescott, being shipped to Halifax, Saint John, West Saint John, Montreal and any other St. Lawrence port east of Montreal. That rate is for grain to be exported only.
With respect to flour the program freezes the rail rate on export shipments from any point east of Thunder Bay, the aforementioned ports.
The reason this program came into being was that back in the early 1960s the railways wanted to increase their rates for movement of these grains and flour. It was argued at the time, obviously very effectively, that those increased rates would price Saint John and Halifax out of the market. What was saved by a subsidy in the 1960s will be ended by the elimination of the subsidy in the 1990s if and when this bill receives third reading in this House, is passed by the other place and proclaimed.
It was felt important to maintain the rates at a fixed level so that eastern rates would remain competitive. This program has been beneficial primarily to Halifax

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
and Saint John but by no means is it an insignificant component for the port of Thunder Bay, nor is it an insignificant component for the maritime community along the Great Lakes, the shipping companies who move grains from Thunder Bay to other ports, or for the ports along Georgian Bay and Lake Huron. They, too, have had most of their existence created by the at and east program, as I will explain in a few moments.
Of all the grain moved through Saint John, 95 per cent moves under the at and east program while 67 per cent of grain moved through Halifax moved through the at and east.
With respect to flour, virtually all flour moved through the two ports moves at at and east rates. Flour amounts to approximately one-third of all general cargo handled at Halifax and 7 per cent of general cargo at Saint John.
In 1988 there were 944,719 tonnes of grain and flour moved under the at and east rate, of which approximately 90 per cent moved via the ports of Halifax and Saint John as their final Canadian ports. The cost to the taxpayers on an annual basis is $32 million, but if we look at its impact the Halifax-Dartmouth Port Development Commission says that the "economics of grain traffic at the port in 1988 amounted to $25.9 million in revenues and 263 jobs, while flour traffic resulted in $28.4 million in revenues and 220 jobs".
Quick mathematics tells me that there was a profit made for those communities and for the taxpayers. For a cost of $32 million, well over $50 million of revenue and wealth was created in the port of Halifax-Dartmouth alone. If we add the impact to Saint John, the impact to the ports along the Great Lakes, the impact to the port of Thunder Bay, to the railroads, to the shipping companies, to the farmers, I would say that this has been a very good investment by the taxpayers of Canada. We have created employment from Saskatchewan through to the Atlantic Ocean. We have kept people working, who in turn have paid taxes, and have purchased goods and services in their communities.
So I would say that a subsidy of $32 million a year is not a drain, not an expenditure that contributes to the
deficit, but it is an investment in the long-term viability of the farmer, the flour mill operator, the shipper, the port worker, the elevator operator. Because the grain is for export purposes, it assists Canada in its foreign trade balance, ensuring that this wonderful product that we grow on our prairies and in Ontario and Quebec can be exported to feed others in other parts of the world.
However, the government is prepared to throw all that away. In the name of deficit reduction, in the name of harmonization, and as part of the over-all plan to eliminate subsidies because they are evil-much like they did with the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement-all of these jobs, all of the stability is placed at risk. Is there not a better way to protect the livelihood of the producers and of those who move and process these grains? Perhaps there is, but it certainly has not been found yet.
We heard earlier from the chairman of the transport committee, who expressed his concern that the government of the day had not come up with any alternatives, had not met the requests of the people of Atlantic Canada who were looking for what he called offsets. Not one of the items that he mentioned has been dealt with in any way. I do not necessarily agree with his suggestions, but clearly it does indicate the failure of this government to balance out its desire for deficit reduction with the desire for Canadians to keep working.
A moment ago I talked about the benefits, particularly to the Atlantic Canada ports. Let me talk a bit about the ports in Ontario who depend on the at and east program for their survival. For some, like Collingwood, the at and east share is only 3.2 per cent of their operations. However, at Midland, 34 per cent of the shipments that they handle are at and east; Owen Sound, 30 per cent; Port McNicoll, 87 per cent or 232,936 tonnes over a five year average are handled by that port; Sarnia, nearly 13 per cent of the grain that they handle comes under the at and east; Prescott, nearly 18 per cent and so on.
This is not just a benefit for Atlantic Canada. This is clearly a benefit for those small port communities along the Great Lakes. We have already heard reports of those elevators being in jeopardy.
April 30, 1990

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if we check the record we will find that one of them has already closed since the illegal termination of the at and east rates last summer.
The other interesting thing that seems to be be ignored in this debate-people will say shipping by water is cheaper, and yes it is. If I had my druthers, all of the bulk commodities moving from the prairies would move through Thunder Bay and be placed on a vessel and transported down the seaway rather than going by rail. It is more efficient from the point of view of energy, and more efficient from the point of view of the environment. It just makes so much more sense. Plus, there is a spin-off of creating a lot of jobs in my constituency, which would certainly go down well in Thunder Bay.
But what people do not understand is that towards the end of the season when the freeze-up begins in the Welland Canal area, the lakers from Thunder Bay are still able to carry export grains to the bay ports. They basically fill up those elevators in the late fall and early winter. That is the grain shipped under the at and east program throughout the winter months to provide a continuous flow for Halifax and Saint John. That will now cease to exist. Instead of having a mix of water and rail east of Thunder Bay, we are going to lose both, because we know that the grain will not be moving.
This is not the first attack on the system. Thanks to the Western Grain Transportation Act passed by the previous Liberal administration just before they were defeated in 1984, there was a section which unwittingly changed the balance in Canada. It changed from a market-driven distribution, and by that I mean it did not matter which direction the grain was going to flow, the price was the same. But under the WGTA, shipments through the west coast are treated, in effect, differently than they are through the east coast. The rail rates are equalized and distributed according to distance between the farm gate, Thunder Bay and Churchill on the east and Vancouver and Prince Rupert on the west, but the water component east of Thunder Bay, and even the rail component east of Thunder Bay is not included. So there was always an extra cost.
The Canadian Wheat Board, which has a mandate to get the highest price for the lowest cost for the producer, something that we fundamentally agree with, is forced to maximize the west coast. This leaves Thunder Bay with
Government Orders
the residuals and Churchill with very, very little, even to the point where grain is being exported through the port of Vancouver destined for Egypt and they have to go through the Panama Canal to make that delivery. It is because of the WGTA.
I realize that is not the bill before us, Mr. Speaker, but I thought it was important in the context of the shift away from the traditional water commerce component of the Great Lakes and the shift away from Atlantic Canada and Quebec. As grain movements through the seaway on the Canadian side have gone from 60 per cent of exports going through Thunder Bay and the seaway, we are now down to 30 per cent. That means that Baie Comeau, Port Cartier, Quebec City, Halifax and Saint John are losing valuable vessel traffic. The elimination of the at and east subsidy is only going to make those matters worse. It may mean, for example, that our already dwindling seaway fleet which was 160 or 180 ships 15 years ago, has gone down to 70 or 80 ships currently, with a number of them having been flagged out because there is not enough trade nor is there a positive tax incentive for them to remain in Canada. The reality is that more of those ships are going to be scrapped.
When you take 400,000, 500,000, 600,000 or 900,000 tonnes of grain out of the system there has to be a reduction in the fleet, there is no question about it. I think the government has made a major error. It is trying to play poker at GATT, the General Agreement on Jhriffs and Trade, which is meeting to take a look at agricultural subsidies, to try to develop some kind of rules which are fair. But, when you are playing poker, you do not play your hand or fold before you get to the table. You wait until you are playing those cards before you make your decisions, you do not decide to get rid of a subsidy in advance of being at the table. That is what this government has done.
This government is saying that this is an unfair subsidy and that it should not exist, instead of being able to trade it off when it gets to the table. So we say what about the at and east, what about the EEC treatment and the BICEP program in the States?. The government could do a trade-off for that-if we are going to trade-but you do not throw it away before you even start because the impact is too important.

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
I do not know whether, in this great country of ours, we can ever eliminate some kind of financial assistance to the transporters of our commodities. I say that for one primary reason, the way we are built. We are an extremely long and narrow country when it comes to our population. Distances are very, very great. We produce our grain anywhere from 1,000 to 1,600 miles from our oceans. Argentina, one of our competitors, produces only 100 miles from the ocean. Australia produces at less than 100 miles from its coasts. The United States, with a much larger network of waterways through the Mississippi and other man-made canals are within 100 or so miles of water transport, which I indicated previously is the most efficient, the cheapest and the most environmentally friendly form of transportation of bulk commodities.
We cannot compete on a level playing field because we have to move our bulk commodities thousands of miles just to get to salt water, so that we can then take advantage of the ocean rates and move our goods to the purchasers.
I think the bill is wrong. I know that people in my community feel that it is wrong because they see an ever-declining workforce declining even further. Because of this we will lose jobs in the port, in the elevators, on the railway. We will lose jobs at McDonald's, the comer stores, the restaurants, and the school board. As the jobs decline in one industry, there is a trickle-down effect which means the loss of 2.8 additional jobs for every one job that is lost. That has a major impact on a community which has seen its grain handler workforce go from 1,500 or 1,600 at its peak not too many years ago, to around 700 or 800, if they are lucky, this year, with no end in sight.
I realize I just have a minute or two left. The long-term danger is that if we allow not just Thunder Bay, but the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway to become a residual carrier of our grains, there will come a time when we will have bumper crops again and the port of Thunder Bay will be asked to move upwards of 25 to 26 million tonnes of grain. It will have to rot in the fields because we will not have the elevators, boxcars or the ships to move that amount of grain. The hon. member said, "Just ship it through the U.S.".
The reality is that they too do not have the capacity to move so much grain any more, nor do they have the kind of quality controls that has led Canada to be the No. 1 producer of quality wheat in this world. It is because of our inspection and handling procedures that the Americans cannot touch our No. 1 position. No country in the world will accept grain that has been trans-shipped through the United States as Canadian grain. It is just not acceptable.
Whether it is for Atlantic Canada, the ports on the Great Lakes, the port of Thunder Bay, the men and women who produce the grain on the prairies, or the people that mill and package the flour, I say this bill should be rejected by this House because it will come back to haunt us and the government time and time again.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to debate this motion, which in effect is another one of those cracks that we are starting to get used to, taking down Atlantic Canada.
The at and east subsidy program was cancelled in the second last budget of this government. It was cancelled under the guise of deficit reduction. Coming from Atlantic Canada, forgive me if I question the motives of the government or the reasons given for cancelling such a program. Every time we have turned around since this government has been re-elected in November of 1988, we have another reason why it cannot keep its promises or programs to assist Atlantic Canada.
I have listened to most of the debate today and the debate that has taken place up until this point. Anybody watching would be quite aware of the reasons that the at and east program was put in in the first place. It was was to keep Atlantic Canadian ports competitive in the movement of grain and flour, as were the American ports east of Buffalo, New York. It served us well.
As a result of the at and east program, the Canadian government put a cap on the movement of grain to east coast ports, and we were able to maintain a very viable industry in Atlantic Canada, particularly in the port of Halifax. There were over 220 jobs made directly possible and sustainable because of the at and east program.
We have a flour mill in Nova Scotia. It counted on the grain terminal there for its product. We had a terminal in Saint John, New Brunswick, which was very viable as it provided a lot of jobs in that area, an area that has consistently borne the brunt of economic downturns.
April 30, 1990

They were good jobs. They were healthy. We did not feel that we were getting anything that we should not have received because the government had embarked years earlier on a subsidy program out west. The government did not seem to have any difficulty when it came and told us that it had to rationalize or cut its deficit, explaining that the only place it can cut are the guinea pigs down in eastern Canada, down on the Atlantic.
I am not for one moment suggesting that the government should cut the rail transportation under the Western Transportation Act or the western grain. I am not going to suggest that.
I am not going to suggest that there should be a new benchmark put on the movement of goods down the St. Lawrence Seaway, that everything has to be on cost recovery all the time, because the government of past days has embarked on a transportation policy to ensure that our product was competitive, to ensure that the grain was being shipped from Canadian ports.
When the government felt that, under the guise of deficit reduction, it had to tackle this big problem, did it go after the Western Transportation Act and the subsidies under it? No, and thank goodness for those western ports, for the railroad out west, and for the grain producers.
Did it decide all of a sudden that it had to have increased pilotage fees for the St. Lawrence Seaway for goods that were going down there? Absolutely not. When it came time for the government to address what it thought or said was such a serious problem, it only went one place. It went after the at and east program, the program that was directly benefiting Atlantic Canada, most particularly Halifax and Saint John.
Now that by itself would give reason for great concern, because it appears once again that the government is proceeding with unholy haste to punish people in Atlantic Canada for having the foresight not to elect these guys opposite, at least not very many of them, and for having seen through the very thin veil that they presented of progressivity during the last election campaign. Every time we turn around they are creating another excuse to damage industry in Atlantic Canada. Goodness knows, if there is one industry in Atlantic Canada that does not need the type of pummelling that this govem-
Govemment Orders
ment has given our other industries, it is the shipping industry.
I rose in this House after the last budget and I raised some real concerns about basically a tax on the profits of the ports in this country. I raised a concern that the U.S. ports, particularly the ports of New York, were pouring billions of dollars into facility upgrading, because they wanted to take business from the east coast Canadian ports.
At the same point in time, Canadian Pacific and Canadian National were looking at acquiring lines directly from New Jersey or New York up to the Montreal market, and up to the Toronto and southern Ontario markets. At the same time, we see this government abandoning any responsibility for a national rail link in this country.
I talked to officials from the port of Halifax and they said that things were not good but they did not want to say it too loud and were going to try to work through the system. In trying to work through the system we saw what happened. Shortly after this particular budget and that particular cut-back, a dividend of $100 million is what the finance minister required of the ports on the east coast by way of a tax. They wanted a dividend.
The port of Halifax has been struggling to maintain its competitiveness, particularly as a result of the government's abandonment of a national rail policy. It had to cancel two major expansion projects, which makes it less competitive. The port of Halifax has been a very healthy part of our economy in Atlantic Canada, and at the very time that it is feeling the increased pressures of competition from the Atlantic seaboard ports, particularly the ports of New York, down south of the border, the government comes in with what it considers to be a necessary reduction of subsidy that, God forbid, is only going to affect Atlantic Canada. They have not rethought the rest of their domestic transportation policy or agricultural product transportation policy.
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, we have heard this song before. When we went into the free trade debate, the government was so absolutely adamant that the Prime Minister of the day had to have a comprehensive free trade deal that they showed their hands to the Americans. The Prime Minister said on a nationally televised show that his political future and that of his government depended

April 30, 1990
Government Orders
on his government concluding a comprehensive trade deal with the United States, and the U.S. took them right to the wire at 11.30 at night because they knew what he had said, he had showed his cards, and as a result we got a free trade deal without even the definition of a subsidy in it.
Now as we go through further negotiations on the definition of a subsidy, as the GATT negotiations continue, and the subsidies in the agricultural sector, it appears we have had another little giveaway. The little giveaway that we have had is called the at and east program, which at this point, Mr. Speaker, has already shut down the terminal in Saint John. Fully 60 per cent of the feed grain that is going through Halifax is subsidized grain under this program, 100 per cent of the flour is subsidized and, as I said earlier, there are nearly 300 jobs, 250 jobs at least. In Halifax alone last year before this regressive change came in, 372,486 tonnes of export grain were handled in the port of Halifax.
I just want to let everybody know that we are not talking about a city the size of Toronto where 250 jobs perhaps do not mean very much. We are talking about an area of about 325,000 people.
There were 201,676 tonnes of export flour moved through the port of Halifax in 1988. I was reading a statistic before I came in which I think stated that every tonne of product, of grain or flour that is moved through that port, is equivalent to one stevedore's job.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council came before the transport committee. I am glad that the chairman of the transport committee had the good sense not to wait for the government to get this bill through second reading and referred to committee. That particular committee, under the chairmanship of the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, did an advance examination of the effects of this particular subsidy cancellation and it found out what was happening.
This subsidy was cancelled last year without this bill ever being passed by Parliament, and I should remind all Canadians of that. This government does not even care to hear the full debate on the merits of its legislation. It just goes and introduces it and then cancels it. It knows that once it cancels it, once a grain terminal shuts down, once 100 or 200 people are put out of work, the impact is
gone by the time the bill receives Royal Assent, if it ever receives Royal Assent in the other place.
When the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council went to the transport committee, and I think it was on February 20, it had already talked about the major economic impact. At the port of Halifax, throughput at the Halifax elevator for the coming year in terms of export grain is expected to be no more than 60,000 tonnes. That is down from the last year in the program which was 372,000 tonnes.
The government did not care. It went ahead and introduced the bill last year. It saw it had some trouble on the other side and decided to put it off until the fall. But the impact has already hit Atlantic Canada. The impact on the poultry industry and the livestock industry in Atlantic Canada is going to be severe because of the shutdown of the terminal in Saint John and because of the decreased traffic through the one in Halifax which means that the per unit cost goes up in Halifax. We are going to find that the Atlantic Canadian poultry and livestock producers are going to be at an even worse disadvantage than their counterparts in the industry in Ontario, Quebec and western Canada. Goodness knows, they certainly do not need that. They are having a hard enough time as it is.
The government did not wait for a full investigation as to the impact of what it was doing. It was in such haste to give away another card in the GATT negotiations that it gave us away. It cancelled the program and it has already had its effect.
I listened to the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants earlier, and I have to commend him. I was in my office and I listened to his remarks on television. The member for Annapolis Valley-Hants has the backbone to stand up in this House and stand against the government. He had the backbone to stand up and speak for the people in Atlantic Canada who elected him. I listened to him make a plea to his fellow Conservative members from Atlantic Canada for once not to be led like dogs on a leash, not to be dragged along for fear that somehow they were going to be left out in the cold when the Prime Minister reshuffles his cabinet, and to do what was right and fight this legislation and vote against this piece of legislation.
He did that for a couple of reasons. One reason is that I believe that the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants has a keen understanding of the agricultural industry. He has been around long enough to smell a bad bill. He knows this bill is a very bad bill. He also is a little annoyed that there was a report put into the department
April 30, 1990

back in 1985 by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council and it recommended some alternatives. It recommended some amendments to the at and east bill that would have saved the government a lot of money, at least half of the money that was going into subsidies. It has never even received a reply.
On February 19, in a major effort toward compromise and to try to bring the government to its senses, what did it do? It came in with a set of proposals which should have been acceptable to the government, if the government had not already enacted the regulations last July. The member for Annapolis Valley-Plants was absolutely incensed today, as he should have been. I am incensed, as are other members from Atlantic Canada, that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Committee has not even heard a response, nor has the government uttered a word about the proposals that were put forward on February 19.
My hon. colleague and friend from Halifax West, at the other end of the province right next to my riding, did not seem to have the same gumption to stand up. The last time this was before the House, the hon. member for Halifax West stood up and said, in defending this unconscionable cut, this double standard bill on the way that the east and west coast ports and the St. Lawrence ports are treated in this country, that the at and east subsidy should be cut. Then he challenged the opposition instead to join him in lobbying the government for direct assistance to farmers, the Port of Halifax and operators of the grain elevators. Who, in the name of goodness, does he think he is talking to? He says to his colleagues who are opposing this very bad piece of legislation, and opposing it on good grounds, not to complain that the thing has to be done away with, but help him lobby.
We have seen the effect of his lobby. He is the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board. If he has lobbied, he has had absolutely no success. It was just around that time that the Minister of Finance came in with a budget that in effect took $100 million away from the Canada Ports Corporation and, as I mentioned earlier, caused the cancellation of two major expansion programs in the port of Halifax and is going to make the port of Halifax and every other east
Government Orders
coast port less competitive than its American counterparts.
The hon. member for Halifax West should learn a lesson. The lesson is that sometimes it is better not to be led around by the nose. Sometimes it is better to get off the picket fence and try not to have a foot on both sides of the line and to take a stand on an issue. When you take a stand on an issue, sometimes perhaps that sharp point you get from the fence will alleviate the pain. Perhaps, just perhaps, the pain will be lessened the next time that members such as he have to go to the ballot box and explain the comments he made about how everything is all well and rosy down east with the cancellation of the at and east subsidy.

I am very happy to see that he has come into the House. I have had many of his own constituents call and ask me if I could make any sense at all out of his comments. I told them I had listened carefully to his comments, but as of yet there is not any sense. Perhaps a little later in this debate he will tell us exactly what he means, and also explain why there is a difference between his statements on the at and east subsidy, since he represents a riding near Halifax harbour, and the statements of the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants who seems to have the best interests, not just of the port of Halifax, but of the farmers of Atlantic Canada at heart.
This bill should be defeated. This bill is a thinly veiled attempt to further cut subsidies in Atlantic Canada. If the government is serious about addressing the problems in the grain transportation sector, then it should do it all at once. It should not use Atlantic Canada as a guinea pig, as a sacrifice on the GATT altar, as a sacrifice in the free trade negotiations. It should come up with a policy that recognizes the importance of maintaining the viability of ports like Halifax, not just for the trans-shipment of grain or flour, but make them much more viable than they currently are because of this government's policies.
The last thing I want to see, as an Atlantic Canadian, is this government being allowed to go forward with policies that are going to shut down what should be one of our most prosperous and viable sectors, at the expense, not just of jobs in Atlantic Canada, but also to
April 30, 1990

Government Orders
the great benefit of the ports in the New Jersey and New York areas.
I urge my colleagues opposite from Atlantic Canada to take a page from the book of the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, show some gumption, show a great deal of skill and concern for the people of their area, and vote against this bill.
