speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you very much for this opportunity to dispel some of the myths that the hon. member for Dartmouth has just tried to project on the House of Commons, but I hope not across Canada.
In the first place, the at and east is dead and gone. It was finished June 23, 1988, when people stopped making use of it and the shipments under that subsidy provision stopped. We are here simply putting a finis to a book that has already been written, read and over with.
The member does not understand that. He likes to take the opportunity to get up in the House and spout off on a subject which no longer has any practical application. The at and east is finished. He does not bother to mention that the millions of dollars poured out over a long period of time under the at and east subsidy went to Canadian National Railways. They did not go to farmers, the grain elevators or the port of Halifax. They went to Canadian National Railways. What he is doing is asking the House of Commons to continue to pay more and more money to the Canadian National Railways because of the trickle down effect to the east coast ports, some farmers and some other areas of activity.
Getting rid of the at and east means that we have a new opportunity to accomplish the desirable ends in a direct fashion and not working through some outmoded subsidy. He does not even know that the competition is no longer between the east coast Canadian ports and U.S. ports, which was the origin of the at and east, but it is between Canadian ports. Fortunately, our very efficient port in Halifax can compete against the U.S. ports, but it has a little difficulty competing against the St. Lawrence ports, given the subsidization that they were given over the years by the Liberal government's failure to collect ice fees, providing free ice-breaking, and so on.
That is why we are at a disadvantage, not because of any policies of this government.
It is a shame that a member of Parliament should get up and preach rhetoric and falsehoods to the members of the House of Commons, when he should know better, but he does not know better. He does not understand the at and east. He apparently does not know that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission, representing the three maritime provinces, has said time and time again: "Get rid of the at and east but give us offsets".
That is why I stood up in the House of Commons and said that the at and east is dead. Forget the at and east. Get on with obtaining suitable offsets to accomplish the benefits for the port of Halifax, the grain industry, the feed freight that the farmers require, and all of those things.
I say to him once again, as I complete my remarks, please recognize the simple fact that the at and east is dead. Give it a decent burial and go on to accomplish something in the future for your constituents, and all the people in Halifax. Stop the rhetoric and get on with reality.
Mr. Speaker, certainly I do not need a lecture from the member for Halifax West about the at and east program or representing the people of Atlantic Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Yes, you do. You need a lecture.
You need a muzzle.

My hon. friend from London is issuing a statement that might be more appropriate than anything that has been said in the House today.
I would like to address the comments that were just made by my colleague from Halifax West. I am not a great card player, but I do not think that when you are sitting down and playing poker with the jobs and the livelihoods of hundreds of people in Atlantic Canada that what you say, especially with this government, is that it will do away with the program and we will worry about the offsets later. He is quite correct that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council came up in 1985 and recommended some offsets. When they recommended
April 30, 1990

the offsets, this government did not even have the decency to respond.
The member for Annapolis Valley-Hants said a few minutes ago when he got up in debate in this place that he was appalled. The member for Halifax West should be appalled that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Council once again on February 19 put some proposals forward but this government did not even give it the decency of a reply because this government does not want to listen. It is hell bent on destroying the transportation sector right across this country, particularly in Atlantic Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to stand here in the House today to address Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act, which terminates the at and east subsidy for the movement of grain and flour to eastern Canadian ports.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the impassioned speech of my colleague from Dartmouth, Nova Scotia. Someone might wonder why I, from central Canada, am here speaking on this bill. I am very familiar with Atlantic Canada. I know what is going to happen to the ports in Atlantic Canada and I am very pleased to be speaking.
First, I want to make it clear that we are discussing a bill today at second reading which in reality has already become law. Second reading has not been completed. It has not received committee study. It has not had third reading. It has not had Senate approval. It has not had Royal Assent. This is just another prime example of a government which has absolute contempt for the workings of this Parliament. The subsidy we are discussing today has already been terminated. It was terminated over a year ago. It is a fait accompli.
The arrogance of it is only equalled by other examples set by this same government. In August of 1989, it placed full-page ads in the newspapers across the country which stated that "Canada's federal sales tax system will change. Save this notice". The ad was rebuked by the Speaker of this Parliament. He said at that time it was a contempt of Parliament. Again, this government's arrogance knows no bounds.
The at and east grain and flour subsidy program, which has been in effect since the mid-1960s, was created not
Government Orders
only to offset some of the economic advantages that U.S. eastern ports had over Canadian eastern ports, but also because Canadian farmers needed a place to consolidate their grain shipments for export. As the Hon. Jack Pickersgill said in 1966 when this legislation was being discussed: "One of the aims of the subsidy was to ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of Atlantic ports".
Atlantic Canada had flour mills that needed a steady supply of the grains which were eligible for the subsidy, grains such as wheat, wheat flour, oats, barley, iye, com, buckwheat and soybeans.
The Minister of State for Indian Affairs and Northern Development, who spoke for the Minister of Transport when this bill was referred to the House for second reading, said that the terminating of the subsidy will "stimulate creativity and innovation. It will allow the industry to take advantage of unanticipated sales opportunities, no longer constraining potential cost savings".
Why should we believe this government? Nothing it promises comes true. I do not think that the 1,200 workers whose jobs are connected to Bill C-26 will believe this government either, nor will the 320 transport workers and the 295 who hold milling jobs in western Canada, the 75 workers in Georgian Bay ports, the 85 who hold jobs in Halifax and Saint John, and the 402 workers in central Canada.
This is the same government whose leader said in 1988: "I know something about the maritimes. As one whose first seat in Parliament was Central Nova, I feel something special for Atlantic Canada and its needs". Well, I certainly hope that the Prime Minister never tries to seek a seat in Atlantic Canada again, because I am sure he would never get it.
The government has slashed the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and it has sold out Atlantic fishermen to foreign interests. Now this government has continued to inflict hardship on Atlantic Canada with the cutting of the at and east grain and flour subsidy.
The government says it will save $40 or $60 million by ending the at and east subsidy. Let us not forget the $200 million cut out of crop insurance, $48 million cut out of advance payments for grain, $15 million cut out of the Farm Credit Corporation, $12 million cut from the Canadian Dairy Commission; a total of 339 farm support programs alone in the 1989 budget, and this government talks of saving $40 million or $60 million by cutting the at

April 30,1990
Government Orders
and east program as if it was the sole cut-back in farm subsidy.
All of these cuts come at a time when the government's own figures are showing that for the coming year farm incomes will drop in Canada 39 per cent; 101 per cent in the province of Saskatchewan, 87 per cent in Manitoba. All of this is because of cuts to their industry and this government's disregard for farmers.
The cut-backs for the coming year will see the income drop by $2.6 billion, a drop of 64 per cent. All of these cuts are coming at a time when the United States, our partner in the free trade deal, is getting ready to increase its export enhancement program.
It seems very odd to me that we are cutting back on our subsidies while at the same time our neighbours to the south are increasing theirs. This year the U.S. export enhancement program will see at least $566 million in their export programs.
By withdrawing the at and east subsidy, the markets in Atlantic Canada will now be available for imported grain out of the U.S. and other countries. Yet again Canadian producers will be deprived of another market. Atlantic Canada will have to look elsewhere for its purchases.
The withdrawal of the at and east subsidy will place a heavy burden on livestock and poultry producers in Atlantic Canada and it will take away a traditional market from western farmers.
According to this government, the free trade deal was going to benefit Canadians because it would open up agricultural markets for Canadians. We have seen the regard the U.S. has for Canadian agriculture. It used GATT to gain entrance for its dairy products into Canada and one can only wonder how the Americans will benefit from the terminating of the at and east subsidy.
According to the Canadian Transport Commission, Canadian flour exports will be practically non-existent without the subsidy. The government should realize that the at and east is an important part of processing in Canada. Yet, according to this government, there is a
lack of processing of highly-processed agri-food products here in Canada.
This government continues to contradict itself time and time again. It says we need more processing yet it cuts back on subsidies to enhance processing. This government talks about regional sensitivity and about a viable agricultural industry in Atlantic Canada but it has yet to demonstrate it.
In conclusion, it is time this government stood up for the interests of Canadian farmers. The U.S. is putting in place an export subsidy program while at the same time we are removing ours.
The at and east subsidy must be reinstated and the government should begin to fight for a level playing field. This government must act hastily to resolve the subsidy program before more farmers suffer further devastation.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to again address this bill. I do not propose to go on for too long having addressed the merits of it some time before, but I do want to make a few comments.
First, a few moments ago I listened to the member for Halifax West. I was amazed at the comments he made. I was appalled at his ignorance of the effect that this bill is having on his own riding.
He has got some basic facts wrong in the first place. He said that the program ended June 23, 1988. Well, it did not end June 23, 1988. For his edification, the bill was announced in April 1989 in the budget and the government effectively withdrew the program on July 15, 1989.
This member also talked about competition with the port of Montreal which is correct. The ports of Halifax and Saint John have some difficulty competing with the port of Montreal, that is very true. In fact, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission back in 1985 recognized that point and that is why it put forth a proposal at that time.
If this member was paying any attention to his own riding, he would realize that. For him to stand in the House and make those comments is simply appalling. He should be ashamed of himself at what he is saying.
This bill is simply an example of this government's arrogant attitude to Parliament and its arrogant attitude
April 30, 1990

to this country. It is not surprising. This is the government that has brought in closure or time allocation something like 35 times since it has been in office. It has acted in an arrogant manner in a whole host of areas and this is simply one example.
The fact is that there is a very logical alternative to at and east as it stands now, a proposal that was put on the table in 1985 by the APTC, which is a very well respected organization.
In fact, the member from Halifax West should take the time to have a chat with those people. They might educate him a little bit on their concern for the at and east and their concern for this bill.
The effect this bill is going to have on Atlantic Canada is outrageous. It is going to affect $27 million to $30 million per year for the ports of Halifax and Saint John. It is going to put something like 250 to 300 people directly out of work. The elevator at Saint John is already closed. The elevator at Halifax is in danger of closing. Rail crews will be laid off, longshoremen, maintenance workers, elevators workers all laid off. Dover Flour Mills is on the verge of closing.
The member from Halifax West will appreciate knowing that Dover Flour Mills is now effectively out of the commercial flour market because of the loss of this program. In fact, if the Halifax elevator closes, and it may well close in the near future, then Dover Flour Mills will very likely close. If the Halifax elevator closes, it is going to have a devastating effect on the livestock industry, the poultry and hog industries in Atlantic Canada. In Atlantic Canada alone, the poultry industry is a $125 million a year industry.
In Atlantic Canada, despite the good efforts they have made with respect to growing their own feeds and grains in that area, they are still dependent upon western grains. When this program is gone, if the Halifax elevator closes, the storage facilities will be reduced. I do not know what the member's alternative is to storage facilities for the agricultural industry in Atlantic Canada if the Halifax elevator closes. The ripple effect is outstanding, especially when we have a fishing industry that is in desperate straits.
I was in Nova Scotia last week. While the fishing industry is having a very difficult time, things are not going too badly in the Annapolis Valley. People are are doing better than other areas. One wonders with the bill
Government Orders
this government now has before the House whether it is its objective to drive Atlantic Canada into poverty. If it is, it they is doing very well and has been very successful.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Wheat Board has indicated that they like having ice-free ports in Atlantic Canada, at Saint John and Halifax. Certain customers, Cuba for example, would prefer to pick its grain up from Halifax or Saint John as opposed to Montreal. But all things being equal, if there are no ice-free ports, then they may just go elsewhere. There is concern that the western producer may lose markets. The ripple effect is outrageous.
The thing that is so frustrating about this bill, is that there is an alternative. It has been on the table for five bloody years and this government never paid attention to it. In fact, when the minister rose in the House to make her speech about this bill, she did not know anything about it. If this government paid a little more attention to the people of this country-
She has the same problem.

-it would go a lot farther.
I just want to indicate that this bill will be going to a legislative committee. I hope the legislative committee will be making a thorough examination of this bill and hearing a number of witnesses and coming back to the government with its alternative. Perhaps the member for Halifax West would appreciate being part of that. I hope he is, because it would be very good for him to learn something.
I want to compliment the member from Annapolis Valley-Hants. He knows the situation. He has had the courage to stand up in this House and say that he is going to oppose this bill. I think that takes a lot of courage, especially in light of how this government handles people who even make any indication of opposing the government. Heaven forbid. The government never makes a mistake. I commend the member for that. I think it is very courageous for him to do that. I wish the member from Halifax West would consider such an alternative.
In conclusion, the legislative committee will be looking at this bill and coming back with some recommendations. There are some very good recommendations. There is a very good alternative on the table. If this government will look at it, it will cut the cost of the at and east program in half. It will keep the ports of Halifax and Saint John viable. It will retain the jobs and it will be

good for Atlantic Canada. It will be good for western Canada. It will be good for all of Canada.
